summary: This informational ICNRG document gives functions and design considerations for a Name Resolution Service in Information-Centric Networking. Such a service translates an object name into other information, such as a locator or another name, to forward the request.

eli5.summary: In a network where you ask for things by name, something must turn the name into where to find it. This document discusses how to build that helper.

questions: how does icn name resolution work
subtitle: How to translate persistent data names into network locations in Information-Centric Networking.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking names data by content instead of by the server hosting it, enabling seamless caching and producer mobility. But to fetch data, the network must translate a content name into a location where that content can be retrieved. This name resolution problem is one of the most important design challenges in ICN.
tldr.mechanism: A Name Resolution Service (NRS) translates persistent content names into locators, alternative names, metadata, or next-hop information. The RFC describes three approaches: explicit name resolution (separate from routing), name-based routing (integrated with forwarding), and hybrid methods. It covers required functionalities (supporting heterogeneous names, producer mobility, scalable routing) and design considerations (response time, accuracy, fairness, scalability, security).
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides guidance for ICN architects. Name resolution remains unsolved in ways that differ from the centralized DNS model of today's Internet; different ICN architectures make different trade-offs between complexity, scalability, and robustness.

today: RFC 9138 is an informational product of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It is not a standard and describes research considerations, not deployed systems. Various ICN projects (NDN, CCNx, PURSUIT, MobilityFirst, NetInf) implement different NRS approaches guided by these principles.

sections.title: From Host-Centric to Information-Centric Networking
sections.content:
Today's Internet is host-centric: you identify servers by IP address and ask for a file on that server. Information-Centric Networking (ICN) flips the model: you ask for the data by its content name, regardless of which server holds it or where that server is. ICN is location-independent—the same name refers to the same content whether it is at the origin server, cached by a network router, or replicated on another continent.

This shift enables powerful features: content can be transparently cached anywhere in the network (improving latency and reducing backbone traffic), producers can move without breaking URLs, and consumer mobility is naturally supported (just re-request the content after moving networks).

But it introduces a critical problem: Name resolution. Given a content name, how does the network find a copy of that content? In today's Internet, DNS answers this for server names. In ICN, name resolution must handle named data objects that are spread across the network, cached, moved, or replicated. This document defines what a Name Resolution Service (NRS) is and what it must do.
sections.eli5: The new Internet could work by asking for documents by name instead of by server. But first you need a way to find where that document is hiding.

sections.title: Three Approaches to Name Resolution
sections.content:
An NRS translates a content name into other useful information: a locator (a network address), another name (for multi-step resolution), metadata (caching policy, security parameters, alternative sources), or next-hop information (where to send the request next). Three main approaches exist:

Explicit Name Resolution: The NRS is a separate overlay system, like DNS. A consumer queries the NRS: 'where is this content?' and the NRS returns locators. Examples: DONA, PURSUIT, MobilityFirst, NetInf. Advantages: controlled update propagation (only the NRS network, not all routers), potential for guaranteed resolution. Disadvantages: NRS node failures can break content lookup even if the content exists.

Name-Based Routing: Name resolution is integrated with routing. Each router maintains a table mapping name prefixes to next hops. A request propagates through the network (usually by flooding) until it reaches a router with the content or a copy. Examples: NDN, CCNx. Advantages: no centralized system, routing tables can discover cached copies. Disadvantages: flooding can be expensive, scalability challenges.

Hybrid: Combine the two. For instance, start with name-based routing; if it fails, fall back to explicit resolution. Or use explicit resolution to find coarse forwarding paths, then name-based routing for fine-grained discovery.
sections.eli5: You can have a name lookup service like DNS (explicit), or have every router help find content (name-based routing), or mix both approaches (hybrid).

sections.title: What an NRS Must Support
sections.content:
The RFC identifies seven key functionalities:

  • Heterogeneous name types: Flat names (e.g., random IDs), hierarchical names (like URLs), attribute-based names—the NRS should work with any naming scheme.
  • Producer mobility: When a content producer moves to a new network location, the NRS must track the new location. Consumer mobility is naturally supported (re-request after moving), but producer mobility requires the NRS to map names to current producer locations.
  • Scalable routing: The number of content objects could be enormous. The NRS must help routers scale; hierarchical names help via aggregation (one routing entry covers many objects), or the NRS can maintain an overlay that reduces routing table size.
  • Off-path caching: Content cached at arbitrary network locations (not on the request path) is hard to discover via name-based routing. The NRS must advertise replicas so they are discoverable.
  • Nameless objects: Content with only a hash (no name). The NRS must resolve from hash to locator or name.
  • Manifests: Large files represented as collections. The NRS resolves manifest names to locate the manifest, which then lists content names to fetch.
  • Metadata: Beyond locators, the NRS can return rich metadata: available protocols, security parameters, caching hints, and alternative sources.
sections.eli5: The NRS needs to handle different kinds of names, track where producers move, help routers not get overloaded, find cached copies, handle big files split into pieces, and provide extra information about how to fetch data.

sections.title: Design Considerations for an NRS
sections.content:
Implementers must balance multiple design dimensions:

  • Response time: Name resolution should complete within a round-trip time to the NRS server, with reasonable upper bounds for delay-sensitive applications (industrial IoT, telemedicine).
  • Accuracy: The NRS must return correct name-to-locator bindings that are up-to-date. Transient cache additions/evictions need not trigger NRS updates, but producer moves must be propagated quickly.
  • Guarantee: The NRS should resolve successfully with high probability (e.g., five nines availability) if the content exists in the network.
  • Fairness: All content should be served fairly regardless of popularity or producer.
  • Scalability: The NRS must handle billions of devices and zettabytes of content (10^21 bytes). Adding NRS servers should transparently increase capacity with minimal disruption.
  • Manageability: NRS nodes are added and deleted dynamically; management should be automated.
  • Deployability: The system must be deployable at network edges and cores for low-latency resolution.
  • Fault tolerance: NRS server failures should not significantly impact resolution; the system must recover and restore state.
  • Security and privacy: Name mappings must be confidential (access control, encryption), servers and mappings must be authenticated, and the system must resist denial-of-service attacks and protect user privacy (NRS queries should not leak information about what users are requesting).
sections.eli5: An NRS must be fast, accurate, reliable, fair, able to handle huge scale, manageable, deployable, resilient to failures, and secure against attacks and privacy breaches.

sections.title: Security and Privacy in Name Resolution
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that name resolution is security-critical. Confidentiality requires access control and encryption to prevent unauthorized parties from seeing name mappings (especially sensitive in IoT). Authentication is needed at three levels: NRS servers must authenticate themselves and each other to prevent impersonation; producers must authenticate to prove they can modify records; and mapping records must be verified to prevent pollution with false data.

Integrity protections prevent malicious modification of name mappings. An attacker who corrupts the NRS could redirect content requests to fake servers, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks or denial of service.

Resiliency and availability matter against denial-of-service: the NRS should isolate the impact of attacks (a compromised NRS domain should not break the entire system), and fast recovery mechanisms are essential.

These requirements set NRS apart from today's DNS, which emphasizes availability over secrecy (DNS queries are public). An ICN-style NRS must be much more careful about who can read mappings and who can update them, especially in sensitive domains like healthcare IoT or industrial control systems.
sections.eli5: An NRS must keep name mappings secret from unauthorized users, prove that servers and content producers are real, prevent attackers from lying about where content is, and keep working even under attack.
